bib.title: DIET: Lightweight Language Understanding for Dialogue Systems

question: How well can a lightweight joint intent and entity model do on dialogue NLU, and does it need large pre-trained language models?
hypothesis: Large pre-trained models are not needed for dialogue NLU; a modular architecture with sparse features and optional embeddings can match or beat them (stated as a surprise in the abstract).
contributions: Introduce DIET, a configurable multi-task transformer for intent classification and entity recognition that mixes sparse n-gram features with optional pre-trained dense embeddings
Study the effect of ConveRT, BERT and GloVe embeddings and of a mask loss
Show state of the art on NLU-Benchmark even without pre-trained embeddings, and better than fine-tuned BERT at about 6x less training time

method.summary: DIET featurizes tokens with sparse one-hot and character n-gram (n<=5) features plus optional frozen dense embeddings (ConveRT, BERT, GloVe), runs a 2-layer transformer with relative position attention, predicts entities with a CRF and intent with a dot-product similarity loss, plus an optional masked-token loss. Evaluated by 10-fold CV on NLU-Benchmark and on ATIS and SNIPS.
method.task: joint intent classification and entity recognition

datasets.name: NLU-Benchmark (Liu et al. 2019b)
datasets.split: 10 folds, each 9960 train / 1076 test; some utterances appear in multiple folds; fold 1 used for hyperparameters with 250 train utterances held out as dev

datasets.name: ATIS
datasets.split: split of Goo et al. 2018 as used by Chen et al. 2019

datasets.name: SNIPS
datasets.split: same as Chen et al. 2019; 700 training examples used as dev

models.name: DIET
models.architecture: sparse+dense featurizer, 2-layer transformer with relative position attention, CRF entity head, dot-product intent head, optional mask loss
models.init_from: none for the transformer; dense embeddings frozen from ConveRT, BERT or GloVe

other.mask rate: 15% of tokens: 70% mask token, 10% random, 20% kept (as printed)

models.name: BERT fine-tuned inside DIET
models.architecture: BERT in the featurization pipeline, whole model fine-tuned

models.name: Joint BERT (Chen et al. 2019)
models.architecture: BERT with [CLS] intent head and token slot head

training.objective: L_total = L_I + L_E + L_M (dot-product intent loss, CRF negative log-likelihood, masked-token dot-product loss); any term can be switched off
training.batch_size: increased incrementally from 64 to 128; balanced batching
training.dropout: applied to sparse features (rate not stated)
training.regularisation: dropout on sparse features, mask loss, growing batch size
training.hardware: 4 CPUs, 15 GB memory, one NVIDIA Tesla K80
training.wall_clock: about 1 hour on fold 1; 10 hours for all 10 folds (sparse + ConveRT); 60 hours for all 10 folds with BERT fine-tuned
training.seeds: 10 independent models, one per fold, averaged (NLU-Benchmark); 5 runs averaged (ATIS, SNIPS); seeds themselves not stated

inference.decoding: intent: dot-product similarity ranks all intent labels; entities: CRF

metrics.name: micro-averaged F1 (also P and R) on NLU-Benchmark
metrics.definition: intent as multi-class; entity true positive if predicted and gold spans overlap and labels match

metrics.name: intent accuracy and entity micro-F1 on ATIS/SNIPS
metrics.definition: entity counts only on exact span and label match (stricter)

eval.protocol: 10-fold average on NLU-Benchmark following Vanzo et al.; mean of 5 runs on ATIS and SNIPS; +/- values printed; no significance test

evidence.quote: The batch size increased incrementally from 64 to 128

evidence.where: No parameter count is printed anywhere in the paper

results.claim: Fine-tuning BERT inside DIET on all 10 NLU-Benchmark folds takes 60 hours versus 10 hours for DIET with frozen ConveRT plus sparse features (the 'six times faster' ratio).
results.setup: NLU-Benchmark, all 10 folds, DIET with fine-tuned BERT vs DIET with frozen ConveRT + sparse features; hardware stated once for the paper: 4 CPUs, 15 GB, one NVIDIA Tesla K80. Baseline is BERT fine-tuned inside DIET, not a standalone BERT classifier.
results.quote: takes 60 hours, compared to 10 hours for DIET with embeddings from ConveRT and sparse features
results.note: Abstract and conclusion say 'about six times faster' / 'six times faster'; the ratio is derived from 60/10.

results.claim: DIET with sparse + frozen ConveRT (no mask loss) reaches intent F1 90.18 vs 89.67 for fine-tuned BERT inside DIET, a 0.51-point gap the paper calls on par.
results.setup: NLU-Benchmark, mean over 10 folds (one model per fold), +/- is as printed (0.53 vs 0.48)
results.table: Table 4, rows Fine-tuned BERT and sparse + ConveRT, column Intent F1
results.note: Gap is inside one standard deviation.

results.claim: On entities, DIET sparse + ConveRT scores 86.04 F1 vs 85.73 for fine-tuned BERT inside DIET.
results.table: Table 4, rows Fine-tuned BERT and sparse + ConveRT, column Entities F1
results.note: Text says it 'outperforms' on entities; 0.31 gap is well inside the std (1.01, 0.91).

results.claim: Best DIET (sparse + ConveRT, no mask loss) beats HERMIT on NLU-Benchmark intents by over 2 points absolute.
results.setup: NLU-Benchmark, 10-fold mean; HERMIT numbers from Vanzo et al. 2019
results.table: Table 1, rows HERMIT and sparse + ConveRT, column Intent F1

results.claim: Entity F1 of best DIET vs HERMIT.
results.quote: Our micro-averaged F1 score on entities (86.04%) is also higher than HERMIT (84.74%).

results.claim: DIET with only sparse features and no pre-trained embeddings, with mask loss, already beats HERMIT on NLU-Benchmark (intent 88.19 vs 87.55; entities 85.12 vs 84.74).
results.setup: NLU-Benchmark, 10-fold mean, sparse features + mask loss, no dense embeddings
results.table: Table 3, row 2 (sparse, no dense, mask loss), column Intent
results.note: Check marks for sparse/mask columns were lost in text extraction, so the row-to-configuration mapping is inferred from row order and from the text ('Adding a mask loss improves performance by around 1% absolute').

results.claim: Pre-trained embeddings benefit measured as gap between best config and sparse-only+mask: about 2 points intent F1 (90.18 vs 88.19) and about 0.9 entity F1 (86.04 vs 85.12).
results.setup: NLU-Benchmark, 10-fold mean; gap is the reader's subtraction from Table 3, not a number the paper prints
results.table: Table 3, row 2 and row sparse + ConveRT without mask, column Intent
results.note: Abstract says 'no clear benefit to using large pre-trained models'; the gain is from ConveRT (conversation-specific, small), not from large LMs. BERT dense features were worse than GloVe.

results.claim: Adding mask loss improves sparse-only DIET by around 1 point on both tasks.
results.quote: Adding a mask loss improves performance by around 1% absolute on both in-tents and entities.
results.note: Quote kept as printed in the cached text (hyphenation artefact).

results.claim: Contextual BERT embeddings used frozen as dense features perform worse than GloVe; authors hypothesise BERT needs fine-tuning for dialogue.
results.setup: NLU-Benchmark ablation, Table 3 (BERT rows 84-88 intent range vs GloVe 88-89)
results.quote: Interestingly, using contextual BERT embeddings as dense features performs worse than GloVe.

results.claim: Joint training helps entities a lot (86.04 vs 82.57 F1 single-task) and hurts intents slightly (90.18 vs 90.90).
results.quote: the micro-averaged F1 score of entities drops from 86.04% to 82.57% when entities are trained separately
results.note: Best single-task intent config used ConveRT with no transformer layers.

results.claim: On ATIS and SNIPS, sparse-only DIET is within 1-2 points of Joint BERT.
results.setup: ATIS and SNIPS, 5 runs averaged, BILOU tags, exact-span entity match; Joint BERT from Chen et al. 2019
results.table: Table 5, rows Joint BERT and sparse*, column ATIS Intent
results.note: SNIPS entities: 95.10 vs 97.00 (1.9 gap); text claim 'within 1-2%'.

results.claim: Inference takes about 80 ms per utterance.
results.setup: hardware as in training setup (4 CPUs, 15 GB, K80); not stated whether CPU or GPU was used for inference
results.quote: At inference time we need around 80ms to process one utterance.

results.claim: Training DIET on fold 1 of NLU-Benchmark takes about one hour.
results.quote: Training our model on the ﬁrst fold of the NLU-Benchmark dataset takes around one hour.
results.note: 10 folds at ~1 h is consistent with the 10 h figure in Table 4.

limits: No parameter counts reported for DIET or any baseline.

The six-times speed ratio compares against BERT fine-tuned inside DIET, not a standalone BERT classifier, on a K80 GPU machine from 2020; it covers all 10 folds, and the setup does not say which device ran inference.

Intent gain over fine-tuned BERT is 0.51 points, within one std; the headline 'no clear benefit' from pre-training is for ConveRT/GloVe (small) versus BERT used frozen, and the authors concede ConveRT sparse gives the best intent F1.
Hyperparameters were tuned on fold 1 of NLU-Benchmark only; on ATIS and SNIPS DIET is 1-2 points below Joint BERT.
Joint training slightly hurt intents (90.90 single-task vs 90.18).
Frozen BERT features were worse than GloVe; fine-tuned BERT was only tested inside DIET.
No learning-rate schedule, dropout rate, seeds or parameter counts stated; no statistical test.
